messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Vikram remembered the road before he could ever find the words. When the state convoys rolled through his homeland, they did not ask for names; they simply seized men at dusk and dragged them toward unmarked ditches. He had fled with his wife, and decades later built a quiet life as a naturalized American, but the sudden violence left no coherent narrative, only disconnected pieces that refused to fit together. Over the years, those fragmented memories refused to stay in the past. When a delivery truck backfired down his street, the auditory shock of the car sound would instantly pull him back to those headlights. The memory of that flight did not merely return; it dictated his present. Fearing that the past would consume him, he began to constantly scan his surroundings for signs of threat, pacing the perimeter of his pottery studio, watching the driveway, and steering clear of any situation that might make him feel happy or hopeful, as if joy would only make the sudden return of those flashes more devastating. Encountering these triggers quickly fractured his sense of self. When a police cruiser idled near his studio gate, the authority presence would send his heart hammering against his ribs, reinforcing his belief that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him. The constant vigilance he felt necessary to survive those years now made him hypersensitive to every siren and every funeral he passed on his daily walks. He was certain that if he relaxed his guard, he would be utterly unable to cope with even the slightest upset. This low coping belief, in turn, magnified the threat of every ordinary stimulus; because he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, even the distant wail of a hearse or the sight of a neighbor’s memorial service became unbearable warnings of imminent capture. The cycle tightened as the months turned into years. His conviction that he could not cope forced his mind back to the fragmented, vivid memories of the road, as if the only way to survive the present anxiety was to prepare for the old danger. In response, his avoidance habits only deepened his sense of incompetence. By routinely avoiding conflict with his wife whenever she gently suggested they visit a community center, and by constantly checking the locks and the street outside his workspace, he inadvertently proved to himself that he was helpless without his routines. This avoidance of positive events and interpersonal friction made him increasingly reactive to authority figures and car noises, which then cemented his negative appraisals of his own fragility. He was trapped in a corridor of his own making. Now, at seventy-five, Vikram sat on his workshop stool, his hands stained with dry clay, watching his wife fold laundry in the adjacent room. The silence of the house felt heavier than any threat he had known. He had finally agreed to come see a therapist after his daughter insisted his withdrawal was no longer just age or caution. He sat hoping for relief from the exhausting perimeter checks, but his deepest fear was that the diagnosis itself would confirm his worst suspicion: that he was permanently broken. He did not want to be a patient; he wanted, above all, to prove that he could still manage the quiet life they had fought so hard to build.
